title: Pattern Matching with Regular Expressions

# Pattern Matching with Regular Expressions

`grep`, `sed`, and `awk` each accept patterns as input — but up to now, the patterns used were mostly literal strings like `staging` or `DEBUG=`. Regular expressions (regex) extend this: instead of matching fixed text, you describe the *shape* of what you want to match. A pattern like `[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}` matches any seven-digit phone segment without naming every possible number.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/regex.svg)

The core regex ideas are shared across all three tools, but default regex modes differ (`grep`/`sed` use basic regex by default, `awk` uses extended regex). Learning the building blocks once still gives you a common language for filtering with `grep`, substituting with `sed`, and querying structured records with `awk`.

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Use anchors (`^`, `$`), character classes (`[a-z]`, `[0-9]`), and quantifiers (`+`, `?`, `{n,m}`) in patterns
- Enable extended regex with `-E` to use `|`, `+`, `?`, and `()` without escaping
- Reformat and extract text in `sed` using capture groups and backreferences
- Filter `awk` records by field content using `~` (matches) and `!~` (does not match)

## The Scenario: Auditing User Data at `Poridhi.io`

The security team is running a monthly audit. They have two files: a user registry export and a server event log. Both contain real data with inconsistent formatting — phone numbers entered in four different formats, mixed-case patterns, IP addresses mixed in with hostnames. The audit requires:

1. Finding all failed login attempts, including external IPs
2. Extracting activity by specific users
3. Standardizing phone numbers to a single format
4. Identifying users with non-company email addresses

| What | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `regexlab/users.csv` | User registry with inconsistent phone formats and mixed email domains |
| `regexlab/events.log` | Server event log with timestamps, severity levels, usernames, and IPs |

## Part 1: Regex Building Blocks

Before running any commands, here is the syntax used throughout this lab:

| Element | Syntax | Matches |
|---------|--------|---------|
| Literal | `abc` | Exactly `abc` |
| Start anchor | `^` | Beginning of a line |
| End anchor | `$` | End of a line |
| Any character | `.` | Any single character except newline |
| Character class | `[abc]` | One character from the set: `a`, `b`, or `c` |
| Negated class | `[^abc]` | Any character *not* in the set |
| Range | `[a-z]` | Any lowercase letter |
| Zero or more | `*` | The preceding element, 0 or more times |
| One or more | `+` | The preceding element, 1 or more times (native in ERE/`awk`; use `-E` in `grep`/`sed`) |
| Zero or one | `?` | The preceding element, 0 or 1 times (native in ERE/`awk`; use `-E` in `grep`/`sed`) |
| Exact count | `{n}` | The preceding element, exactly `n` times (native in ERE/`awk`; use `-E` in `grep`/`sed`) |
| Range count | `{n,m}` | The preceding element, between `n` and `m` times (native in ERE/`awk`; use `-E` in `grep`/`sed`) |
| Alternation | `\|` | Either the left or right expression (native in ERE/`awk`; use `-E` in `grep`/`sed`) |
| Grouping | `(...)` | Captures a group (native in ERE/`awk`; use `-E` in `grep`/`sed`) |
| Backreference | `\1`, `\2` | Refers back to the 1st, 2nd captured group (in `sed`) |

The `-E` flag enables **extended regular expressions** for `grep` and `sed` — it removes the need to backslash-escape `+`, `?`, `{n}`, `|`, and `()`. `awk` already uses extended regex syntax in its patterns.

In this lab, `grep`/`sed` commands use `-E` whenever ERE-only operators are used; `awk` examples do not need `-E`.

## Part 2: Setting Up the Environment

### Step 1: Create the Working Directory

```bash
mkdir -p regexlab
```

### Step 2: Create the User Registry

```bash
cat > regexlab/users.csv << 'EOF'
id,username,email,phone,status
U001,alice_johnson,alice@poridhi.io,555-123-4567,active
U002,bob.smith,bob.smith@poridhi.io,5551234568,active
U003,carol123,carol@poridhi.io,(555) 234-5679,inactive
U004,dave_brown,dave@gmail.com,555-345-6780,active
U005,eve-davis,eve.davis@poridhi.io,5553456781,active
U006,frank99,frank@yahoo.com,555 456 6782,inactive
U007,grace_lee,grace@poridhi.io,555-567-6783,active
U008,henry_w,henry@poridhi.io,5555676784,active
U009,iris123,iris@outlook.com,(555) 678-6785,active
U010,jack.turner,jack@poridhi.io,555-789-6786,inactive
EOF
```

Notice the phone column has four formats: `555-123-4567`, `5551234568`, `(555) 234-5679`, and `555 456 6782`. The email column mixes `poridhi.io` accounts with `gmail.com`, `yahoo.com`, and `outlook.com`. These inconsistencies are what the audit needs to find and fix.

cat > regexlab/events.log << 'EOF'

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image.png)

## Part 3: Filtering with `grep` and Extended Regex

### Step 1: Anchors — Match at the Start or End of a Line

`^` pins a pattern to the beginning of a line. `$` pins it to the end.

Find all ERROR entries in the event log:

```bash
grep "^2024-01-15.*ERROR" regexlab/events.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-1.png)

`^2024-01-15` ensures the match starts at the beginning of the line — this prevents matching a log message body that happens to contain a date. `.*` means any characters in between.

Find all log lines that end in a local private IP (192.168.x.x):

```bash
grep "192\.168\.[0-9]*\.[0-9]*$" regexlab/events.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-2.png)

`$` at the end anchors the pattern to the line's end — these are successful logins from the internal network. The `\.` escapes the dot so it matches a literal `.` rather than any character.

Count internal logins vs total login events:

```bash
grep -c "logged in from" regexlab/events.log
grep -c "192\.168\.[0-9]*\.[0-9]*$" regexlab/events.log
```

### Step 2: Character Classes and Quantifiers

Character classes match one character from a defined set. Quantifiers control repetition.

Find all WARNING events where usage is above a percentage threshold:

```bash
grep -E "[0-9]+%" regexlab/events.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-3.png)

`[0-9]+` matches one or more digits. The `+` requires `-E` (extended regex). Without `-E`, you would need `[0-9][0-9]*` to express "one or more digits."

Find usernames that contain only letters, digits, and underscores (valid Linux usernames):

```bash
grep -E "^U[0-9]{3},[a-zA-Z0-9_]+" regexlab/users.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-4.png)

`[0-9]{3}` matches exactly three digits. `[a-zA-Z0-9_]+` matches one or more alphanumeric characters or underscores. Lines where the username field contains a dot or hyphen (like `bob.smith` or `eve-davis`) will not match.

Find usernames that contain a dot or hyphen — non-standard characters for Linux:

```bash
grep -E "^U[0-9]{3},[a-zA-Z0-9]*[.\-][a-zA-Z0-9]" regexlab/users.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-5.png)

### Step 3: Alternation — Match Multiple Patterns

`|` (pipe) in extended regex means "or". Use it to match any of several alternatives in a single pass.

Find all ERROR and WARN events:

```bash
grep -E "ERROR|WARN" regexlab/events.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-6.png)

Find users with external email addresses (non-poridhi.io domains):

```bash
grep -E "@(gmail|yahoo|outlook)\." regexlab/users.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-7.png)

`(gmail|yahoo|outlook)` is a group containing three alternatives. The outer parentheses are not strictly necessary here but make the alternation scope explicit. `-E` enables both `|` and `()` without backslashes.

Count how many users have external email addresses:

```bash
grep -cE "@(gmail|yahoo|outlook)\." regexlab/users.csv
```

Find all failed login attempts from external IPs (not starting with 192.168 or 10.0):

```bash
grep "failed login" regexlab/events.log | grep -vE "from (192\.168|10\.0)\."
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-8.png)

`grep -v` inverts the match — it returns lines where the pattern does *not* match. Piping two `grep` commands: first filter for failed logins, then exclude internal IP ranges.

**Why it matters**: Alternation replaces running multiple `grep` commands. A single `ERROR|WARN|CRITICAL` pass over a multi-gigabyte log is much faster than three separate passes.

## Part 4: Reformatting with `sed` Capture Groups

Capture groups record what was matched and let you rearrange or reuse it in the replacement. A group is written as `\(...\)` in basic sed or `(...)` with `-E`. The first group is referenced as `\1`, the second as `\2`, and so on.

### Step 1: Reformat Dates

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/regex-date.svg)

The event log dates are in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Audit reports require `DD-MM-YYYY`. Use three capture groups to reverse the order:

```bash
# Preview
sed -E 's/([0-9]{4})-([0-9]{2})-([0-9]{2})/\3-\2-\1/' regexlab/events.log | head -3
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-9.png)

Each `([0-9]{2})` captures two digits. `\1` is the year, `\2` the month, `\3` the day. The replacement `\3-\2-\1` reorders them. The original string `2024-01-15` becomes `15-01-2024`.

Apply in-place:

```bash
sed -Ei 's/([0-9]{4})-([0-9]{2})-([0-9]{2})/\3-\2-\1/' regexlab/events.log
head -3 regexlab/events.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-10.png)

### Step 2: Normalize Phone Numbers

The users file has four phone number formats. All of them contain exactly 10 digits — the formatting characters differ. The goal is `NNN-NNN-NNNN`.

First, strip all non-digit characters from the phone column to get the raw 10-digit number:

```bash
# Preview — remove parentheses, spaces, and hyphens from the phone field
sed -E 's/(\(([0-9]{3})\) |([0-9]{3})[-. ]?)([0-9]{3})[-. ]?([0-9]{4})/\2\3-\4-\5/' regexlab/users.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-11.png)

This pattern is complex, so let's break it down:

| Pattern piece | What it captures |
|---------------|-----------------|
| `\(([0-9]{3})\) ` | Area code with parentheses and trailing space: `(555) ` — captures `555` as `\2` |
| `([0-9]{3})[-. ]?` | Area code without parentheses, optional separator — captures `555` as `\3` |
| `([0-9]{3})[-. ]?` | Middle three digits — captures as `\4` |
| `([0-9]{4})` | Last four digits — captures as `\5` |

The replacement `\2\3-\4-\5` combines whichever area code group matched (only one of `\2` or `\3` will be non-empty) and adds dashes in the standard positions.

A simpler two-pass approach is often easier to maintain. First collapse the phone field to 10 digits, then insert dashes:

```bash
# Pass 1: normalize phone field to 10 digits (works for all 4 input formats)
sed -E 's/^([^,]*,[^,]*,[^,]*,)\(?([0-9]{3})\)?[ .-]?([0-9]{3})[ .-]?([0-9]{4})(,.*)$/\1\2\3\4\5/' regexlab/users.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-12.png)

Here, `^([^,]*,[^,]*,[^,]*,)` captures the first three fields and the comma after them as `\1`. The phone number is captured in groups `\2`, `\3`, and `\4` without any formatting. The rest of the line (status) is captured as `\5`. The replacement reconstructs the line with just the digits in the phone field.

```bash
# Pass 2: insert standard dashes into the now-uniform 10-digit phone field
sed -E 's/^([^,]*,[^,]*,[^,]*,)\(?([0-9]{3})\)?[ .-]?([0-9]{3})[ .-]?([0-9]{4})(,.*)$/\1\2\3\4\5/' regexlab/users.csv \
  | sed -E 's/^([^,]*,[^,]*,[^,]*,)([0-9]{3})([0-9]{3})([0-9]{4})(,.*)$/\1\2-\3-\4\5/'
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-13.png)

Here, the second `sed` command takes the output of the first and applies a simpler pattern that assumes the phone field is now exactly 10 digits. It captures the three segments of the phone number and inserts dashes between them.

Verify the output — all phones should now be `NNN-NNN-NNNN`:

```bash
sed -E 's/^([^,]*,[^,]*,[^,]*,)\(?([0-9]{3})\)?[ .-]?([0-9]{3})[ .-]?([0-9]{4})(,.*)$/\1\2\3\4\5/' regexlab/users.csv \
  | sed -E 's/^([^,]*,[^,]*,[^,]*,)([0-9]{3})([0-9]{3})([0-9]{4})(,.*)$/\1\2-\3-\4\5/' \
  | awk -F',' '{print $4}'
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-14.png)

Here, the `awk` command at the end extracts just the phone column to verify the formatting.

Save the normalized file:

```bash
sed -E 's/^([^,]*,[^,]*,[^,]*,)\(?([0-9]{3})\)?[ .-]?([0-9]{3})[ .-]?([0-9]{4})(,.*)$/\1\2\3\4\5/' regexlab/users.csv \
  | sed -E 's/^([^,]*,[^,]*,[^,]*,)([0-9]{3})([0-9]{3})([0-9]{4})(,.*)$/\1\2-\3-\4\5/' \
  > regexlab/users_clean.csv

cat regexlab/users_clean.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-15.png)

**Why it matters**: Real-world data is never clean. Phone numbers, postal codes, dates, and identifiers arrive in a dozen formats. Capture groups let you decompose the input, discard the formatting, and reconstruct it in the form your system expects — without writing a script.

## Part 5: Field-Level Matching in `awk`

`awk` applies regex in two ways: `/pattern/` tests the whole line, and `$field ~ /pattern/` tests a specific field. The `!~` operator inverts the test.

### Step 1: Match Whole-Line Patterns

Regex between `/` slashes applies to the entire record:

```bash
# Print all ERROR lines
awk '/ERROR/' regexlab/events.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-16.png)

```bash
# Print all lines containing an IP address
awk '/[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+/' regexlab/events.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-17.png)

### Step 2: Match a Specific Field

Use `$field ~ /pattern/` to test only the value of one field:

```bash
# Print users whose email is NOT a poridhi.io address
awk -F',' 'NR > 1 && $3 !~ /poridhi\.io$/' regexlab/users_clean.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-18.png)

`$3` is the email column (1-indexed). `!~` means "does not match". `poridhi\.io$` anchors the domain to the end of the field — the `\.` escapes the dot so it matches a literal `.` rather than any character.

```bash
# Print only active users with a poridhi.io email
awk -F',' 'NR > 1 && $3 ~ /poridhi\.io$/ && $5 ~ /^active/' regexlab/users_clean.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2014/images/image-19.png)

Combining two field conditions lets you intersect criteria — a task that would take two `grep` passes becomes a single `awk` statement.

**Why it matters**: Field-level regex testing in `awk` lets you combine pattern matching with arithmetic in a single pass. Instead of filtering with `grep` and then aggregating with `awk`, you express both conditions inside one `awk` program — fewer commands, one pass over the data.

## Conclusion

In this lab, we used one shared regex vocabulary across all three tools:

- `grep -E` filtered lines using anchors, character classes, quantifiers, and alternation — reducing thousands of log lines to the events that matter
- `sed` capture groups decomposed structured strings (dates, phone numbers) and reassembled them in a different format — without any scripting language
- `awk`'s `~` and `!~` operators applied regex at the field level — combining pattern matching with grouping.

The regex building blocks from Part 1 — anchors, character classes, quantifiers, alternation, and groups — are the same elements you write in Python, JavaScript, or any other language that supports regex. The difference here is that you applied them directly on the command line, without writing or running a program. A pattern you understand once is a pattern you can use everywhere.
